question: During a cardiovascular examination of an 8-year-old girl, you auscultate a soft (grade 2/6) midsystolic murmur at the upper left sternal border that disappears when the child stands up. There is no thrill, no radiation, and all other cardiovascular parameters are normal. What is the MOST likely conclusion?

answers.text: This murmur is pathological and echocardiography is urgently needed to rule out pulmonary stenosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulmonary stenosis produces an ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border but is typically harsh, grade 3+ or has a click, and does NOT disappear on standing. A murmur that softens or disappears on standing is a key feature of innocent murmurs — venous return decreases, reducing flow through the right heart.

answers.text: This is most likely an innocent (functional) murmur that does not require echocardiography

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Features pointing to an innocent murmur: soft (grade 1-2/6), midsystolic, no thrill, no radiation, and the murmur decreases/disappears with standing or Valsalva (reducing preload). Common innocent murmurs in children include Still's murmur (vibratory, LLSB), pulmonary flow murmur (upper LSB), and venous hum (infraclavicular, disappears on lying). No investigation beyond a careful clinical assessment is needed for a classic innocent murmur in an otherwise well child.

answers.text: The disappearance of the murmur on standing rules out any cardiac pathology, including atrial septal defect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The behaviour on standing is a useful clue but not a definitive rule-out for all pathology. Certain ASDs can have subtle murmurs that vary with position. The full picture — including fixed split S2, right ventricular heave, and clinical context — must be assessed. However, in this case the classical innocent murmur features make ASD less likely.

answers.text: A systolic murmur at the upper left sternal border in any child always requires referral to a paediatric cardiologist

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Not all murmurs require specialist referral. Innocent murmurs are present in up to 50-80% of children at some point and are a normal examination finding. Referral is warranted if the murmur is pathological (diastolic, grade 3+ with thrill, pansystolic, harsh, with abnormal S2 splitting or cardiac symptoms). A classic innocent murmur in a well child can be managed in primary/general paediatric care.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key innocent murmur features: grade 1-2/6, systolic only, no thrill, no abnormal heart sounds, and most importantly — changes with posture (decreases on standing because preload falls). A murmur disappearing on standing strongly favours innocent over pathological.

Well done. Innocent murmur features: soft, systolic, no thrill, no radiation, varies with posture (decreases on standing). Still's is vibratory at LLSB; pulmonary flow murmur is at upper LSB. These are normal examination variants.
